title: Nineteenth-century brass equatorial refractor on a mahogany tripod

subject.summary: An approximation of the portable three-inch refractors the London and York makers built in the 1840s-1880s, after the Troughton & Simms and Cooke pattern: a long lacquered brass tube with its dew shield and objective cell, a finder scope, a rack-and-pinion focuser, and a German equatorial head with an hour circle, a declination circle and a turned counterweight, carried on a folding mahogany tripod. Not a copy of any one instrument.

identity.feature: a long slender lacquered brass tube with brass bands, a knurled objective cell and a flaring dew shield
a German equatorial head: inclined polar axis, graduated hour circle, declination circle, turned counterweight
a folding mahogany tripod with brass shoes, ferrules and knuckles, braced by a chain spreader
a small finder scope on two brackets, parallel to the main tube
a rack-and-pinion focuser with twin knurled knobs and a drawtube eyepiece
long slow-motion rods with knurled knobs hanging from the mount

next: the saddle is still a flat plate crossing the tube: give it a curved cradle with a strap over the tube
the hour circle needs engraved numerals and a needle that touches its rim (only the dec circle has a scale and index)
the slow-motion rods should be straight screw rods with knurled knobs, not bowed wires
the chain spreader wants drawn links and each leg a visible knuckle block; the legs still read as dowels
at hero scale the head's drum, latitude quadrant and two circles still crowd: separate them further along the polar axis
engrave a maker's name on the objective cell (the reference cell carries one; this instrument is left unsigned on purpose)
